title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
summary: As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors. Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials. Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company disclosed the incident on October 22 , and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21. “AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise. They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables. In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. Th

title: AI-related job creation to outpace losses by 2030, says Gartner
summary: Wider use of AI within organizations will lead to more jobs being created than are lost by 2030, according to Gartner. Around 10.6 million jobs will be added globally (excluding China and India) by the end of the decade, with 8.9 million lost, according to a Gartner report — a net increase of 1.7 million jobs. At most, around 1.8% of the workforce will experience job losses attributable to AI during this time period, Gartner predicts. At the same time, a total of 5 million jobs will cumulatively be deferred during this period. This refers to jobs that “would otherwise have been created, but where AI is used as an excuse to restrain hiring,” according to Gartner’s report . Gartner considers deferred jobs as separate from jobs lost. “Job deferrals were the first effect felt from AI,” said John Lovelock, Gartner distinguished VP analyst and chief forecaster, with “companies holding off hiring open positions until the effects of AI projects were known.” A recent KPMG survey of 400 US CEOs showed that 89% expect to increase headcount over the next three years, which KPMG US CEO Tim Walsh linked to AI adoption in an Axios interview last month. For now, though, job losses attributed to AI outpace those created, according to Gartner’s study. During 2026, there were 2.2 million jobs lost due to AI, and 1.6 million gained. Lovelock expects the situation will change in the coming years, however, as organizations see greater success with AI deployments. “This will reverse once AI is through the Trough of Disillusionment ,” he said, in reference to Gartner’s Hype Cycle framework . Gartner The number of jobs deferred is also forecast to fall in the coming years. During 2026, 1.3 million people experienced a delay in hiring, down from 2.1m last year, according to Gartner’s forecast, with 400,000 jobs forecast to be deferred during 2030. title: Claris Harbor could turn Mac fleets into on-prem AI servers
summary: It feels quite appropriate that one of Apple’s more interesting AI deployments may not come from the company itself, but from its more business-focused subsidiary, Claris, still better known to many as FileMaker. What we know is limited: It intends to release an app that uses Apple Silicon Macs to create a private AI server. What Claris is promising The company, famous for its database software for the enterprise, has initiated a private preview of what sounds — at least on the surface — like something worth watching for enterprise users seeking to achieve AI insights from their data. The product is called Claris Harbor, and the company says it “turns the Apple silicon computers you own into a private AI server.” To achieve this, Harbor leans steeply into the powerful performance packed inside Apple Silicon : “Set up an endpoint in minutes on a single Mac.” It also makes use of the existing features of Macs that have already made them so popular among people deploying OpenClaw. “When you want to run larger models, connect multiple machines over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory on hardware you control,” Claris said. It also says you can set up an endpoint on a single Mac — one of your Macs becomes an AI server for everyone else . Your Macs. Your AI Put this together and you have an Apple solution built around the part of the company with extensive enterprise and database experience that offers one of the emerging holy grails of business-class AI — powerful, scalable AI that can work on confidential and protected data on-premises, on-device, and in confidence. “Data and prompts stay strictly within your physical Mac hardware,” the company promised. While Claris doesn’t claim it, it’s not hard to imagine those banks of Macs already deployed in business being used as AI clusters overnight before returning to normal business use in the morning. title: Alexandr Wang: from the data behind AI to Meta’s frontier models
summary: Alexandr Wang’s career connects two often separate stories about artificial intelligence: the human work that makes data useful, and the organisation of laboratories that build frontier models. Raised in Los Alamos by physicist parents, he showed an early aptitude for science before leaving MIT and co-founding Scale AI with Lucy Guo in 2016. Scale turned data preparation and evaluation into a major business. Meta’s 2025 minority investment then brought Wang into its own AI leadership. This profile follows that transition through his upbringing, the company’s formation, its defence-planning work and his responsibilities at Meta. It also examines what the headline transaction actually meant, why labelled data is important without being the sole basis of AI, and how the contribution of researchers and annotation workers fits into the story. A dated chronology, a biographical record and linked sources place the individual within the wider institutions that shaped his influence.
author: The Bible of AI

title: Ripple-65B Preview: open weights, evidence and auditability
summary: Ripple-65B Preview brings a dense, 65-billion-parameter model to the open-weight landscape, with a particular emphasis on coding and terminal-based tasks. This profile examines what Ricursive Intelligence has actually released, how its chip-design business relates to the model, and what external evaluations can establish. It separates the laboratory’s benchmark claims from Plotly’s data-analysis assessment and DuelLab’s provisional game-based results. It also distinguishes announced company funding from the model’s reported development expenditure. Public weights, configuration and inference code support inspection, but they do not by themselves disclose the complete training data or establish that a generated reasoning trace faithfully explains a decision. The assessment therefore considers licensing, reproducibility, hardware requirements and scientific support separately. It is a documentary review of public evidence, not an Editorialia performance test or a certification of safety, general intelligence or complete transparency.

title: AWS boosts Bedrock AgentCore runtime compute capacity to speed up AI agent development
summary: AWS on Thursday said that it was upgrading the runtime layer of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with greater compute capacity, more efficient memory utilization, and faster startup times to help enterprises deploy and scale AI agents more quickly and cost-effectively. The greater compute capacity includes support for up to four times more compute than the previous version, with each session now supporting up to eight virtual CPUs (vCPUs) and 32GB of memory, the hyperscaler said in a statement. In addition, the runtime supports container images of up to 10GB, it further said, adding that these upgrades will allow developers to run more demanding agent workloads, including large codebase compilations, browser-driven workflows, and local model inference. As for memory utilization, the new updates will enable AgentCore runtime to reclaim unused memory within minutes of an agent releasing it and allow idle agents to scale to zero. This will help enterprises reduce the cost of running agents, particularly those that spend considerable time waiting for model responses, tool calls, or human intervention, the hyperscaler said. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this can reduce memory consumption per session by up to 68%, it added. Separately, in order to support always-on agents, the hyperscaler has introduced baseline pricing as part of the updates. Baseline pricing, according to the hyperscaler, sets a minimum memory allocation per session while allowing workloads to burst up to four times that baseline when additional capacity is needed. That predictability in pricing will allow enterprises to maintain always-on agent sessions without paying for peak capacity upfront while retaining the flexibility to scale when demand increases, it said. title: Google’s Gemini Decisions API to handle up to 1,000 questions per request
summary: Google has announced Gemini Decisions API, offering developers a way to handle routine decisions in AI applications without generating text responses, weeks after OpenAI launched a competing service. Powered by the company’s new Gemini Decision 1 model, the API allows developers to evaluate up to 1,000 questions in a single request. Unlike conventional generative AI models that produce responses token by token, the system assigns probabilities to specified options, allowing applications to make decisions without waiting for a generated answer. Developers can use the API to check whether a condition is met or select an option from a predefined set. It can also score inputs against a rubric, allowing applications to evaluate the degree to which an input meets specified criteria. The API supports multimodal inputs, including images, audio, and video, with a context window of up to 256,000 tokens. Developers can use the resulting confidence scores to determine when an application should proceed automatically or refer uncertain cases for further review. Google said the API delivers end-to-end latency of 150 to 250 milliseconds in tests involving contexts of up to 16,000 tokens, with performance remaining relatively stable across one to 100 questions. The company has priced the API at $0.10 per million input tokens, without additional output-token charges. “Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens),” Google said in its announcement. Google is already using the technology in its Gemini Notebook product to route queries to different AI models based on the complexity of each request. According to the company, the approach lowered latency for everyday queries by as much as 40%. Google said it is also using the API in Search to detect adversarial behavior involving Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, extending its use beyond model routing to security-related decisions

title: The sketch Qwen refused to write: How abliteration restores local AI control
summary: As consumer-grade hardware makes hosting local AI practical for both developers and enterprises, many are discovering that popular open-weight models come with hardcoded safety filters and state-mandated biases. In this article, I will show how to use abliteration — a representation engineering technique — to surgically delete refusal vectors from the Qwen 3.8 27B model without expensive fine-tuning or full retraining. I stumbled into this barrier firsthand while running a simple experiment. As a massive SNL fan, I decided to explore what an SNL sketch would look like in China by asking the model to write political satire. While Qwen happily mocked American politics (“ The National Apology Tour “), it threw a hard, canned refusal the moment I asked for the exact same sketch criticizing the Chinese government. We trust open-source software because it is audited by millions of users, but projecting this trust onto AI models requires a careful distinction between open-source and open-weight architectures. True open-source models disclose their training codebase, inference code, and original datasets. For example, OpenCLIP is a genuine open-source model capable of making sense of visual data, which I recently demonstrated in a project building a zero-cloud photo deduplicator . Conversely, advanced large language models (LLMs) rarely qualify under the strict open-source definition; they are simply open-weight. They provide only the final compiled result: the weights. There is fierce competition in this space, with some of the most capable models, like Qwen 3.8, originating from China and outperforming competitors. But running these black-box weights locally comes with inherent strings attached. The anatomy of an AI refusal As powerful as they are, open-weight models pose distinct risks. title: Exploring Microsoft’s AI foundation models
summary: When Microsoft started to deploy AI models in what is now its Foundry platform, it was building on its partnership with OpenAI. OpenAI was able to use Azure infrastructure to train its models, and in return, Microsoft became the first commercial partner to use them. Azure OpenAI has been a successful product for both businesses. But as more organizations got access to OpenAI models, Microsoft’s stable of models grew to include not only OpenAI’s, but also models from Anthropic and Hugging Face, as well as models from Meta, Mistral, and DeepSeek. At the same time, Microsoft has continued to offer its own Cognitive Services models for computer vision and text processing, as well as the Phi series of efficient lightweight models for use on the edge. With access to more than 11,000 different models , Foundry has proven to be a useful way to build modern AI-based applications, offering many agent-focused features, including tools to ground models using Microsoft’s graph-based IQ data sources. But one key element has been missing — Microsoft’s own large-scale frontier models. Microsoft AI has a long history It’s not that Microsoft is new to developing its own AI models. Microsoft Research has been a hub for deep learning for much of the last decade, with models that regularly top benchmark tables. But it hasn’t taken the same general-purpose approach as Anthropic, OpenAI, or even Google, instead producing more focused models. Now Microsoft has begun to roll out its own foundation models as part of its Microsoft AI (MAI) program. With a focus on offering lower token cost than competitors, MAI has spotted a gap in the market. It’s a sensible move to make, too. The days of free and low-cost tokens have gone, never to return, as hyperscale vendors look to recoup the massive multi-billion-dollar investments they’ve made in AI data centers. title: llm-gemini 0.37
summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.
